newsitem.title: UK: Eurotunnel safety report follows bumpy route.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel safety report follows bumpy route.

text.p: A safety commission sharply criticised Anglo-French channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel on Tuesday for its handling of a November fire that injured eight people. Key dates in the Channel tunnel project are:
1964. France and Britain decide to build tunnel underneath the Channel and accept outline proposals by contractors in 1971.
1974. France ratifies treaty on tunnel but Britain's newly elected Labour government cancels project in 1975. Companies are compensated for initial work.
Sept 11, 1981. French President Francois Mitterrand and British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher announce new studies into a tunnel.
Jan 20, 1986. Out of four proposals, the Eurotunnel twin-bore rail tunnel, built by the TransManche Link (TML) building consortium, is selected.

May 12, 1987. European Investment Bank (EIB) lends one billion pounds ($1.5 billion) to the project, later backed by one billion pounds from banks and 770 million pounds from a Eurotunnel share issue.
July 29, 1987. French and British leaders grant Eurotunnel a 55-year operating concession.
Dec 1, 1987. Tunnelling begins at British side.
Oct 2, 1989. Eurotunnel says project costs have increased by 40 percent to seven billion pounds ($10.5 billion) and it will have to seek more funds.
Jan 8, 1990. Contracting consortium TML takes Eurotunnel to court over unpaid bills.
Feb 16, 1990. French court orders Eurotunnel to pay 62 million pounds ($93 million) to TML. Bank of England calls for secret talks on cost overrun dispute.
May 28, 1990. EIB provides 300 million pound ($448 million) loans and banks later lend further 1.8 billion pounds.
Dec 1, 1990. British and French tunnel workers shake hands under the channel as the two sides break through.
Dec 3, 1990. Eurotunnel raises 566 million pounds ($846 million) in rights issue.
June 28, 1991. Main tunnelling work completed.
Nov 6, 1991. Loan from European Coal and Steel Community.
Nov 27, 1992. Crucial bank waiver on 6.8 billion pounds of debt.
May 17, 1993. Channel Tunnel terminal opens at London's Waterloo station.
June 20, 1993. Test train makes first tunnel trip.
Oct 11, 1993. Eurotunnel seeks one billion pounds ($1.49 billion) extra cash and puts total costs at 10 billion pounds, twice its original estimate.
Jan 1994. Banks agree to fresh financing.

April 21, 1994. Eurotunnel says needs a further 1.2 billion pounds ($1.8 billion) in new funds, plus enough to cover additional interest costs to carry it through the first few years of operation until revenues can support operating and finance costs.
May 6, 1994. Official opening of tunnel by French President Francois Mitterrand and Britain's Queen Elizabeth.
May 19, 1994. "Le Shuttle" freight truck service opens.
Nov 14, 1994. Eurostar passenger service officially opens.
Dec 22, 1994. "Le Shuttle" car and passenger service opens.
April 10, 1995. Eurotunnel reports 1994 loss of 387 million pounds and warns: "Our debt-service costs may overwhelm us."
Sept 14, 1995. Eurotunnel freezes debt payments for up to 18 months.
April 22, 1996. Reports net loss of 925 million sterling and warns cashflow may never pay off debts and interest.
Oct 7, 1996. Eurotunnel unveils details of a massive debt restructuring, including plans to give its 225 creditor banks a 45.5 percent equity stake. Plan subject to shareholder approval.

Nov 18, 1996. Fire breaks out aboard a train carrying 29 trucks through tunnel, sending eight to hospital and causing tens of millions of pounds damage. Tunnel closed to passenger and freight traffic.
Dec 4, 1996. Eurostar passenger service resumes through tunnel.
Dec 21, 1996. London-Paris express stranded in tunnel for almost three hours.
April 3, 1997. Eurotunnel admits to avoidable delays in dealing with November fire, but says not due to mechanical or systems failure.

April 24, 1997. Eurotunnel reports 1996 net loss of 685 million pounds ($1.1 billion), says will be forced to seek insolvency if shareholders fail to approve the restructuring plan on its nine billion pounds ($14.6 billion) of debt. Company also seeks a 999-year extension of its operating licence.
May 7, 1997. France formally asks Britain to extend Eurotunnel operating concession, which expires in 2052.

May 13, 1997. Channel Tunnel safety authority sharply criticises Eurotunnel but stops short of demanding a redesign of existing open-sided freight wagons. Says freight service must remain closed until a ruling by an intergovernmental commission later this week.
